strategy.title: No executable plan: the audit workbook has no evidenced purchase price
strategy.why: The only opening's $500 'price' is what the huntr bounty platform pays researchers per valid vulnerability report, not what maintainers pay for an audit workbook; without a price buyers pay, no revenue from the 1,500 reachable projects is established.

alternatives.title: Sell the workbook to maintainers at $500
alternatives.why: Rests on a bounty reward used as a purchase price; maintainers' willingness to pay is not evidenced.

alternatives.title: Submit vulnerability reports to huntr for bounties
alternatives.why: A bounty is a contingent reward for findings, not a sale of the workbook; payout depends on valid findings and approval timing, neither established.

steps.label: Find a published price open-source maintainers actually pay for a dependency audit (or audit workbook), with source and date

quantities.name: workbookPrice
quantities.needs: A published price maintainers pay for a dependency audit workbook

sources.claim: The huntr bounty platform pays security researchers $500 for each valid vulnerability report in an open-source project.
sources.population: Security researchers paid bounties by huntr (not workbook buyers)

sources.claim: 1,500 open-source projects are listed on the bounty registry; each publishes a security contact.
sources.population: Open-source projects on the bounty registry

noPlan.decisiveGap: OFFER_AND_PRICE: the $500 figure is a bounty huntr pays researchers for vulnerability reports, not a price maintainers pay for the workbook, so no evidenced price exists and the 1,500 reachable projects carry no established revenue toward $3,000.
noPlan.resolution: Research a published price maintainers pay for dependency audits (revenueRange question cnd_63cffbb2071a4532ade7), or run a zero-cost priced offer to the published security contacts and record actual paid orders.

excluded.why: Price evidence is a bounty reward paid to researchers, not a purchase price paid by the buyer.
